c.v: is initialised the first time execution reaches its declaration, and never again. Since C++11 that initialisation is thread-safe: if two threads reach it at the same time, one waits for the other. Only the initialisation is protected. Reads and writes after that need their own synchronisation.

You will hear "stack" and "heap" in interviews. They describe how implementations usually provide automatic and dynamic storage, and the standard uses the longer names. Either is fine, as long as you know they mean the same thing.

Dynamic storage is the only kind whose end you control by hand, which is why most lifetime bugs involve it. Modern C++ gives that job to an owner, such as a container or a smart pointer. Later topics cover both.

subs.title: Construction and destruction order: bases, members, locals, statics

c.v: Read this program and write down its output before you look below it:

blocks.text:

  make Base::engine
  Base body
  make Robot::left
  make Robot::right
  Robot body
destroy:
  ~Robot body
  drop Robot::right
  drop Robot::left
  ~Base body
  drop Base::engine

c.v: Construction starts with the base classes, in the order they are declared. Then the members are built, in the order they are declared in the class, and the constructor body runs last. Destruction runs in exactly the reverse order: the destructor body, then the members from last to first, then the bases.
shows both halves: it is the first object built and the last one destroyed.
Locals follow the same idea at the level of a block. They are destroyed at the end of their block, in reverse order of construction. Statics are destroyed after
returns, in reverse order of when their construction finished.
